## Intent

Reaching the bug requires a role the program has written out of scope: owner, admin, operator, guardian, governor. Most programs exclude privileged-role findings in almost these words.

## Detection signals

Signals name the role and the capability ("admin can", "onlyOwner", "requires a privileged signer"). The rule is about the precondition, not the impact — a severe impact reached only by an admin is still privileged-role-gated.

Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against the full text of the
draft finding, subject to the engine rules below.

**Fires when at least one of these matches:**

```text
  \bonly(owner|admin|operator|guardian|governor)
  only (the |an? )?(owner|admin|operator|guardian|governor|curator|manager)
  (admin|operator|curator|manager|owner)[ _]?(cap|capability|role|privilege)
  (admin|operator|owner|governor|guardian) (can|may|could|is able to|has the (power|ability))
  requires? (the |a |an )?(privileged|trusted|admin|elevated) (role|actor|address|signer|action)
  access[- ]control(led)? by (the |)(owner|admin)
  capability[- ]gated
  set by (the |)(admin|owner|operator)
```

## Escape hatches

Suppression patterns that are evidence an unprivileged path exists: demonstrated unprivileged escalation, "any user can trigger", "permissionless", "without any privileged role", a MISSING access check, and a user-held owner or approved operator (the owner of a token or position is not a privileged role). They are scoped to the SENTENCE, not the document: a "permissionless" in an unrelated sentence must not switch the rule off. A separate document-level list suppresses the whole rule when an unprivileged caller steals, drains, or extracts yield. "The owner can set the fee" in another sentence is then context, not the attack. The engine's negation window also treats "missing", "lacks" and "without" as cues, so "missing the onlyOwner modifier" does not fire. "No one but the admin", "nobody except the owner", and "no one other than" are exclusive claims, not negations, and they still fire.

**Suppressed when any of these matches, in the same sentence as the fire:**

```text
  unprivileged (escalation|path|attacker) (is |was |)(demonstrated|shown|proven)
  any (user|caller|attacker) can (trigger|call|invoke|reach)
  permissionless
  without (any )?(privileged|elevated|admin) (role|access|capability)
  \b(token|nft|position|share|lp|deposit|account|vault share) owners?\b
  \bapproved operators?\b
  (missing|lacks?|lacking|no|without) (an? |the )?(access control|access check|role check|auth(ori[sz]ation)? check)
```

**Suppressed from any sentence** when one of these matches, even if `none_of` is sentence-scoped. The match is still negation-aware:

```text
  unprivileged (user|caller|attacker|address|account)[^.]{0,180}(steal|stole|stolen|drain|drains|drained|extract|extracts|extracted|profit|profits|profited|theft|yield)
  (any|every) (user|caller|attacker)[^.]{0,140}(steal|stole|stolen|drain|drains|drained|extract|extracts|extracted|profit|profits)
  steals? (the )?(pending |unclaimed |accrued )?yield
```

## Known false-positive modes

These are the shapes where the rule fires on something it should not. They are the
reason a firing is a prompt to check, not a verdict.

- The unknowing-admin case — a reasonable admin action with a non-obvious destructive second-order effect. The report mentions the admin and is suppressed only if it also argues unprivileged reach.
- A finding where the role is required to *deploy* but not to *exploit*.
- A report about a compromised key, where the role is a consequence of the compromise rather than a precondition of the bug.

## Synthetic examples

Both examples are synthetic. They describe no real report and no real target.

**Fires:** "An admin can set the fee to 100% and brick liquidations."

**Does not fire:** "Any caller can invoke this; unprivileged escalation is demonstrated."

## Corrective action

Check whether an unprivileged attacker can trigger the bug without role compromise. If not: hold. The one escape is UNKNOWING admin harm - a reasonable admin action with a non-obvious destructive second-order effect.

## Changelog

| Date | Change |
|---|---|
| 2026-11-09 | "No one but the admin can" was dropped by the negation window. An exclusive phrase (no one but, nobody except, no one other than) is an affirmation. An unprivileged yield theft that also says the owner can configure a parameter is suppressed for the whole document. |
| 2026-11-06 | "missing the onlyOwner modifier" - the opposite signal, an unprivileged path - was hard-killed. "missing" is now a negation cue, and a user-held token owner or approved operator suppresses the rule. |
| 2026-10-10 | Suppression is now sentence-scoped and requires evidence that an unprivileged path exists. A "permissionless" in an unrelated sentence used to switch the rule off, which is exactly backwards. |
| 2026-10-08 | Introduced with the first catalog commit. |
